topics.title: 22.1.1 Distinguishing Authentication from Authorization
topics.summary: Authentication establishes an identity under a trust mechanism. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a particular action on a particular resource. A successfully authenticated service is not necessarily allowed to read another tenant’s job or force a workflow transition.

topics.chapterTitle: Securing Service Identity and Authorization Boundaries
topics.title: 22.1.2 Preserving Identity Across Service Hops
topics.summary: A gateway can authenticate an external caller and then call a worker under its own service identity. The worker needs to know which claims it may trust and whether it should enforce end-user scope, gateway scope, or both. Blindly forwarding arbitrary user headers can turn the gateway into a confused deputy.

reading.title: 22.3.1 Validating Resource Use Alongside Syntax
paragraphs: A syntactically valid request can still be too large, too frequent, or too expensive. Validate payload length before allocating based on a declared size. Validate domain ranges before arithmetic or database insertion. Apply per-operation resource limits even after authentication.

The wire decoder rejects payloads above 4096 bytes and does not allocate an arbitrary declared length. Keys and integers have explicit limits. These checks reduce the attack and failure surface, but they do not constitute a complete denial-of-service defense for a public service.

reading.title: Engineering case — Preserve authorization through an authenticated gateway
paragraphs: An external client authenticates as tenant A to a gateway. The gateway calls a worker using its service credential and forwards a payload containing tenant=B. If the worker trusts the payload tenant because the gateway connection is authenticated, the client has crossed an authorization boundary through a trusted intermediary.

The gateway must validate the requested resource scope against the verified principal before delegation. The worker must know whether the gateway is authorized to assert end-user scope and how that assertion is protected. A service credential authenticates the gateway; it does not automatically validate every claim the gateway forwards.

One design uses a narrow internal request constructed only after authorization, with an authenticated delegation mechanism and an explicit audience. Another lets the worker independently validate a delegated token. The choice depends on the identity infrastructure, but both require a clear distinction between untrusted request data and trusted claims.

Test a valid identity with a mismatched tenant, a valid tenant with a missing action permission, an expired delegation, and a request arriving through a path that bypasses the expected gateway. A positive test proving that the ordinary client succeeds does not address these cases.

Logging should preserve the decision category and relevant nonsecret identity reference without copying tokens. A support bundle containing bearer credentials can create a new access path during an investigation. Diagnostic convenience must not expand the trust boundary accidentally.

The supplied principal model tests the final policy predicate only. It deliberately does not manufacture authentication from a string. Likewise, the actual loopback application contains no tenant security layer and must not be exposed publicly on the strength of this example.
